body:
@julienw Thanks for the issue! If you're reporting a bug, please be sure to include:
1. The version of ESLint you are using (run `eslint -v`)
2. What you did (the source code and ESLint configuration)
3. The actual ESLint output complete with numbers
4. What you expected to happen instead

Requesting a new rule? Please see [Proposing a New Rule](http://eslint.org/docs/developer-guide/contributing/new-rules) for instructions.

The rule is warning not because of the `forEach`, but because of the outer `for...in` loop. You are creating a new function for each iteration of the outer loop. I think the rule is behaving correctly. It will actually not flag functions inside `forEach`.

Thank you for this issue.

I know that immediate called functions are no problem even if those exist in a loop. But it's too hard to detect whether it's immediate called or not in static analysis. So I guess `no-loop-func` is warning all functions in a loop.

I often write `// eslint-disable-line no-loop-func`, so I think it's inconvenient, though....

> The rule is warning not because of the forEach, but because of the outer for...in loop. You are creating a new function for each iteration of the outer loop. I think the rule is behaving correctly. It will actually not flag functions inside forEach.

Yes I know why the rule is warning. I know it's also happening because I access `result` that's out of the loop.

My proposal here is that we could assume that methods called forEach/map/reduce/etc immediately execute their function parameter. No need for complex static analysis.

This behavior would be behind a new config flag for the rule.
How about only ignoring `[].forEach.call(..., function(){ ... })`? I could get behind that.

Could you explain why you think just because the function is an argument for `forEach` it's fine to use inside the loop? My understanding was that one of the reasons behind this rule was that function creating is expansive, due to creation of new scope. And doing that inside the loop would be even more costly. I'm not sure why does it matter that the function is an immediate call.

What @michaelficarra said. (see also https://github.com/eslint/eslint/blob/master/docs/rules/no-loop-func.md for more explanation)

The doc above says that the code already checks for let-scopped variables. But in my example I'm using a variable that's outside of the `for` scope (`result`), that's why the rule gives a warning.

Yet with forEach and friends there is no issue. (Thinking about the performance is doing premature optimization IMO). Of course I could use `Objets.keys.forEach` instead of `for in` and then the issue would disappear by itself :) Yet I think adding a flag could be useful here.

But again I'm not suggesting to change the default behavior, because I understand some users could want this behavior and the change could be a surprise to them. Yet adding a new configuration flag for the rule would be nice.
@julienw I don't think we'd even need a flag if we limited the exception to what I suggested. Would you be okay with that?
Sorry, I'm not sure I understood the rationale behind your suggestion :)
We can be reasonably confident that, when written that way, we're using the `forEach` from the Array prototype.

@michaelficarra :-1: The utility to maintenance cost ratio for your proposal seems low. Not everyone would think to try that style of invoking forEach and it would have to be called out in docs, and it doesn't really gain all that much. On the other hand, the code to do that isn't super trivial either. I don't much like it, sorry.

Creating exceptions for array methods is far too specific a change for this rule. 

It looks like we already have exceptions for using `let` or `const` loops, so the question is, why is this warning at all right now?
